text: Processors are required to implement cGMP controls that prevent allergen cross‑contact, including controls that are part of the cGMP prerequisite program and sanitation monitoring procedures to prevent cross‑contact in areas such as ingredient handling, processing, storage, and equipment cleaning. [fda_seafood_ch19:2:0]

The final regulation permitting the use of ionizing radiation on raw meat and meat products was issued by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, Food Safety and Inspection Service (USDA/FSIS). [fda_food_code_2026:424:0]

Written environmental monitoring procedures should:  
1. Be scientifically valid and specify whether testing is for Listeria spp. or L. monocytogenes. [fda_lm_rte_2017:41:0]  
2. Identify sampling locations and the number of sites to be tested, ensuring adequacy to assess control effectiveness. [fda_lm_rte_2017:41:0]  
3. Specify the timing and frequency of sample collection and testing, again to determine effectiveness. [fda_lm_rte_2017:41:0]  
4. Detail the test(s) and analytical method(s) used, and the laboratory performing the testing. [fda_lm_rte_2017:41:0]  
5. Include corrective‑action procedures to be followed when Listeria spp. or L. monocytogenes is detected. [fda_lm_rte_2017:41:0, fda_lm_rte_2017:44:2]
Shell eggs packed for consumer use must be stored and transported at an ambient temperature of no greater than 45 °F. [fda_food_code_2026:470:1]
The two primary ways to reduce water activity in foods are (1) product formulation, such as adding salt or sugar, and (2) dehydration (drying). [fda_pchf_ch04:24:0]

The process log for each production line must contain the plant or facility identification, the dates (and when appropriate, the times) of monitoring, the signature or initials of the person performing the monitoring (e.g., operator initials), and evidence of review (i.e., the initials of the PCQI or designee). [fda_pchf_ch06:15:0] [fda_pchf_ch06:14:1]

No. A foreign facility that is required to register under Section 415(a) of the FD&C Act is not required to submit a reportable food report if the reportable food is shipped elsewhere, but not to the United States. [fda_rfr_qa_ed2:30:0]

The FDA recommends that a seafood processor develop a written sanitation standard operating procedure (SSOP) for allergen control that includes: identifying the items to be cleaned (e.g., processing equipment, utensils, food‑contact surfaces); defining a cleaning frequency that reflects the risk of cross‑contact and is consistent with cGMPs; and providing detailed instructions on cleaning protocols, including equipment breakdown, specific chemicals, concentrations, temperature set‑points, and other critical factors for effectiveness. The SSOP should also include monitoring and verification steps to ensure cleanliness and allergen removal. [fda_seafood_app10:1:2]

The regulation of pesticides in food is shared by three federal agencies: the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and the U.S. Department of Agriculture Food Safety and Inspection Service (USDA FSIS)【fda_pchf_ch03:22:1】.

Physical hazards are broadly classified as “hard/sharp” physical hazards and “choking” hazards. Both categories can cause injury to the consumer, including dental damage, laceration of the mouth or throat, laceration or perforation of the intestine, choking, and even death. [fda_pchf_ch03:33:1]

An establishment must identify all possible post‑lethality FCSs as part of its sampling program, the sample size for each FCS, the sampling frequency (e.g., number of samples per month per line) and the total number of samples to be collected routinely, and provide a justification that the sampling frequency is sufficient to ensure effective control of Listeria spp. [fsis_dir_10240_4_r4:13:1]

Cookie Processor B’s corrective action procedures specify that if cookies were baked in an oven that was not at least 350 °F (177 °C), the cookies will be diverted to further processing (e.g., baking for cookie crumbles ingredient production) or to animal food (non‑pet food); maintenance will determine the cause of the low temperature and fix the oven so the temperature is reset to the operating limit of 352 °F (178 °C) before more cookies are baked; and employees will be retrained, if necessary, on the importance of ensuring that the oven temperature has reached the set point before allowing the line to run. [fda_pchf_ch06:24:1]

The Salmonidae family includes the following fish species that may be fed with canthaxanthin or astaxanthin color additives: pink salmon, coho salmon, sockeye salmon, chinook salmon, Atlantic salmon, chum salmon, rainbow trout, cutthroat trout, and brown trout. [fda_food_code_2026:497:0]

Receiving facilities under subpart G of part 117 are facilities that manufacture or process a raw material or other ingredient that they receive from a supplier. Examples include a plant that turns raw agricultural commodities into bagged salads, a mill that turns wheat into flour, or a cookie factory that uses flour, sugar, and other ingredients. These facilities are subject to subparts C and G of part 117. [fda_pchf_ch15:5:1]

Good hygiene practices (GHPs) may not be sufficient when the hazards present in an operation cannot be fully controlled by GHPs alone, requiring additional measures or greater attention to specific GHPs to manage those hazards. [codex_cxc1_1969:14:1]

Melamine is considered a significant chemical hazard that must be addressed in a food safety plan when the ingredient’s country of origin has a history of melamine adulteration. In such cases, the hazard analysis should identify melamine as a potential economically‑motivated adulterant and require a preventive control. If there is no history of melamine adulteration in the country of origin, it is not regarded as a significant hazard for domestic milk products or milk products from that country. [fda_pchf_ch03:27:0]

Waste must be handled so as to exclude contamination of food or potable water, with precautions to prevent pest access. It should be removed from meat‑handling and other working areas at intervals, at least daily, and any receptacles or equipment that have come into contact with the waste must be cleaned and disinfected immediately after disposal. The waste storage area itself should also be cleaned and disinfected at least daily. [fssai_sched4_compendium:82:1]
The recommended volume of primary enrichment transferred from each sponge or swab into the secondary enrichment broth when compositing up to five samples is 0.1 ± 0.02 mL. [fda_lm_rte_2017:84:0]

The RO is responsible for coordinating effectiveness checks and directing FSIS personnel activities. It must determine product distribution, request assistance from Assisting Offices, and decide whether additional consignees should be added to the distribution list. The RO eliminates duplicate consignee listings, uploads the list into APM, and assigns the appropriate number of on‑site and telephone checks using the tables in Attachment 1. It may group checks by special consignee categories and apply the relevant table to each category. Finally, the RO selects a subset of consignees for checks using the selection criteria in Attachment 1. [fsis_dir_8080_1_r8:15:0]

To regain control after a critical limit deviation involving mislabeled allergen information, the following corrective actions should be taken: inspect remaining labels staged for use and remove inaccurate labels from the processing area; review a representative sample of labels in storage, hold and isolate inaccurate labels if appropriate; discontinue use of the label supplier or work with the supplier to ensure corrections are made to prevent recurrence; and modify label procedures as appropriate. [fda_seafood_ch19:9:0]

If maintenance employees cannot be excluded from RTE areas during operations, they should either be required to cease operations until a full cleaning and sanitizing is completed, or they must change outer clothing and any other soiled clothing, use separate tools for raw and RTE areas (or wash and sanitize tools and hands prior to entering RTE areas), and wear only freshly cleaned/sanitized footwear in such areas. [fsis_lm_rte_2014:75:0]
Food employees must vigorously rub the surfaces of their lathered hands and arms together for at least 20 seconds and then thoroughly rinse with clean water. [fsis_sps_guide:75:0]

If a consignee is unsure whether it has handled a recalled product, it should conduct a recall audit check by visiting the storage sites and inspecting the shelf stock to confirm that all recalled product has been identified, removed from areas of use, and properly quarantined or destroyed/corrected. If the recall involves a field correction, the consignee should obtain a copy of the service order or the in‑house biomedical engineer’s response form to demonstrate that the correction was performed. The consignee should document the status of the correction in the remarks section of the FDA 3177 form and, if necessary, notify the FDA recall contact of any uncertainty or need for further guidance. [fda_iom2026_ch07:17:1]

No.  A food‑contact surface that tests positive for Listeria spp. does not automatically make the product adulterated; the product is only considered adulterated if it tests positive for Listeria monocytogenes (Lm)【fsis_lm_rte_2014:118:1】.

If meat and poultry products are cooled slowly after partial cooking that does not reach full lethality, vegetative cells of *Clostridium perfringens* and *C. botulinum* can grow during the cooling period, leading to a higher cell count in the finished product and increasing the risk of food‑borne illness. In some cases, cooling between 120 °F and 80 °F for 3–4 hours can result in 2–3‑log growth of *C. perfringens*, which would exceed the performance standard or target. [fsis_appendix_b_2021:26:0]

Incorporating HACCP principles into routine inspections gives operators constructive input that helps them establish the control system needed to bring foodborne‑illness risk factors back under continuous control. [fda_food_code_2026:593:0]

Recipe management is used as a process control to prevent misformulation of food ingredients, ensuring that excessive amounts of additives, color additives, or GRAS substances are not added beyond their maximum use levels. This control strategy helps avoid chemical hazards that can arise from over‑use of ingredients. [fda_pchf_ch04:29:0]

The FDA guidance identifies intrinsic characteristics that can prevent the growth of *Listeria monocytogenes* in ready‑to‑eat foods, including: a pH ≤ 4.4; a water activity ≤ 0.92; and the presence of one or more inhibitory substances (e.g., sorbic acid, benzoic acid, or naturally occurring antimicrobials from fermentation) that, alone or in combination, act as listeristatic hurdles. These characteristics can be naturally present or deliberately introduced during processing to create a “hurdle” that inhibits *L. monocytogenes* growth. [fda_lm_rte_2017:32:0] [fda_lm_rte_2017:3:0]

Yes, an establishment that relocates will most likely need to repeat the in‑plant validation element of its initial validation because the new location may affect critical operational parameters and require new in‑plant data to support the HACCP system. [fsis_haccp_validation:32:0]

Yes. If a facility receives a shipment, tests a sample, and determines the food is a reportable food, the facility must submit a report even if it rejects the shipment and returns it to the supplier. The facility is considered to have “held” the reportable food because the trailers were no longer in transit once dropped off on the property, making it a responsible party. [fda_rfr_qa_ed2:10:0]

The process approach is a method of applying HACCP in retail and food‑service settings by dividing the many food flows in an establishment into broad categories based on activities or stages in the preparation of the food, then analyzing the hazards and placing managerial controls on each grouping. This approach uses food‑preparation processes common to a specific operation rather than individual food commodities, making it more efficient and useful for retail and food‑service operators. [fda_retail_haccp_manual:17:0] [fda_food_code_2026:585:0]
Intensified sampling is recommended to begin after a second positive Food Contact Surface (FCS) result. [fsis_lm_rte_2014:117:0]
The PCQI must review corrective‑action records within one week of the deviation occurring. [fda_pchf_ch06:53:0]

Cleaning chemicals and other dangerous substances must be stored in containers that are clearly identified and kept separately from food contact areas to prevent malicious or accidental contamination. [fssai_sched4_compendium:44:2]

Irradiation of food in the United States is performed with ionizing radiation from two approved sources: gamma rays emitted by radioactive cobalt‑60 or cesium‑137, and X‑rays produced by high‑energy electron accelerators that strike a heavy‑metal target. These are the only ionizing radiation sources authorized for food treatment under 21 CFR 179.26. [fda_pchf_ch04:13:2]

Cabinets used for the storage of food, or for storing cleaned and sanitized equipment, utensils, laundered linens, and single‑service or single‑use articles may not be located in locker rooms, toilet rooms, garbage rooms, mechanical rooms, under sewer lines that are not shielded to intercept potential drips, under leaking or condensed water lines, under open stairwells, or under other sources of contamination. Cabinets for linens or single‑service/single‑use articles may be stored in a locker room. If a mechanical clothes washer or dryer is provided, it must be located so that it is protected from contamination and only where there is no exposed food, clean equipment, utensils, linens, or unwrapped single‑service and single‑use articles. [fsis_sps_guide:62:0, fda_food_code_2026:129:0]

A facility can be considered compliant with 9 CFR 416.2(d) when condensation is present on a drip pan but has been reduced through fan installation, provided that the establishment has taken reasonable measures to minimize the condensation and that the drip pan’s bottom surface is maintained in a sanitary manner so that any remaining condensation cannot adulterate product. This determination is made by inspection program personnel (IPP) who verify that the condensation is controlled and that the surfaces are kept clean, treating them as if they were food‑contact surfaces. This approach aligns with the guidance that condensation must be controlled to prevent product adulteration, because the establishment has implemented reasonable ventilation measures and continues to maintain sanitary conditions for any residual condensation. [fsis_dir_5000_1_r8:13:0] [fsis_dir_5000_1_r8:12:1]

Sanitation controls must include procedures, practices, and processes that prevent allergen cross‑contact and cross‑contamination from insanitary objects and personnel to food, food‑packaging material, other food‑contact surfaces, and from raw product to processed product. They must specifically address allergen cross‑contact and cross‑contamination. [fda_pchf_ch04:35:0]

A slaughter establishment that is not very low volume must sample cattle, sheep, goats, horses, mules or other equines for generic E. coli at a rate of one test per 300 carcasses, with a minimum of one sample each week of operation. [fsis_dir_5000_1_r8:48:0]  

Very low‑volume establishments that collect samples by sponging must take at least one sample per week, starting the first full week of operation after June 1 of each year and continuing at a minimum of once each week the establishment operates until June 1 of the following year or until 13 samples have been collected, whichever comes first. [fsis_dir_5000_1_r8:48:0]

A HACCP plan is not required for a TCS food packaged using reduced‑oxygen packaging (ROP) in a food establishment—except for fish—if the product is labeled with production time and date, held at the required cold holding temperature, and removed from ROP packaging within 48 hours after packaging at the establishment. [fda_food_code_2026:697:0]

A food product must be **safe and wholesome**—meaning it contains no ingredients that pose a public‑health concern and is free from contamination such as Listeria monocytogenes—so that it can be donated under USDA FSIS guidelines. It must also have **proper labeling** that accurately lists all ingredients, including the Big 9 allergens, and any mislabeling must be corrected with temporary label approval and a “Not for Sale” statement if needed. The product must not be **economically adulterated** under FDA law, which requires that no valuable ingredients are omitted, substituted, or removed, and that no substance is added to increase bulk or weight, reduce quality, or create a misleading impression of value. Finally, the donation must be authorized on a case‑by‑case basis by the standing regulatory agency, ensuring no public‑health risk is present. [fda_food_code_2026:436:1] [fda_food_code_2026:437:0]
The ambient air temperature may not exceed 5 °C (41 °F) for more than 30 minutes immediately after the machine is filled, serviced, or restocked. [fda_food_code_2026:122:1]
The maximum ambient air temperature allowed for refrigerated storage or processing of raw material, in‑process product, or finished product is 40 °F (4.4 °C) or below. [fda_seafood_ch12:17:0]
In the FSIS Listeria guidance, adding 2 % or 3 % potassium lactate to frankfurters inhibited or delayed the growth of *Listeria monocytogenes* during refrigerated storage. [fsis_lm_rte_2014:51:0]
The minimum hold time required in the hold tube during the continuous heat treatment of clear broths and creamed vegetable soups is 2.5 minutes. [fda_pchf_ch06:32:1, fda_pchf_ch06:33:0]
The Registering Authority must issue a license, reject the application, or issue an inspection notice within 60 days from the date of receipt of the application. [fssai_sched4_compendium:5:0]
The acceptable quality limit used for outbreak‑related recalls that are class I with injury is 4.0. [fda_rpm_ch07:120:0]
The minimum temperature required for a handwashing lavatory is 43 °C. [fsis_sps_guide:52:0]
The degree‑hours are calculated from the time needed to reach pH 5.3. [fsis_hazards_controls_2018:59:2]
The maximum time frame allowed between sampling and receipt at an external or internal pathogen testing laboratory is 2–3 days after collection. [fsis_lm_rte_2014:95:2]
The internal temperature of the fish must be maintained at 40 °F (4.4 °C) or below to ensure the ice is sufficient during storage. [fda_seafood_ch12:12:1]
The food‑contact surfaces of cooking and baking equipment must be cleaned at least every 24 hours. [fda_food_code_2026:137:0]
Not found in the provided documents.
The maximum time allowed for the first stage of the two‑part cooling process (from 130 °F to 80 °F) is 1.5 hours. [fsis_appendix_b_2021:23:0]

In a shelf‑life study, FSIS recommends using a storage temperature of **45 °F or higher** to assess Listeria monocytogenes growth, as this “slightly abusive” condition can reveal a <2‑log increase in Lm when an antimicrobial agent is present. [fsis_lm_rte_2014:63:0]
Not found in the provided documents.
The reference internal product temperature used to calculate lethal rates for Listeria monocytogenes is 158 °F (70 °C)【fda_pchf_app3:3:0】.
The guidance recommends that ready‑to‑eat foods be stored at 4 °C (≈40 °F) or below to minimize Listeria monocytogenes growth. [fda_lm_rte_2017:37:2]

A responsible party must submit an electronic report to FDA as soon as practicable but in no case later than 24 hours after determining that an article of food is a reportable food. [fda_rfr_qa_ed2:14:1]
The salsa must be cooked to a minimum temperature of 158 °F (70 °C) and held at that temperature for at least 1.5 minutes. [fda_pchf_ch06:39:2]
The operating limit for baking time is 15 minutes, while the critical limit for baking time is 13 minutes. [fda_pchf_ch06:17:1]
The food must be cooked to a minimum temperature of 63 °C (145 °F). [fda_food_code_2026:686:0]
The maximum cumulative exposure time for Vibrio cholerae growth at 51‑70 °F (11‑21 °C) is 6 hours. [fda_pchf_app3:6:0]
Not found in the provided documents.
FSIS should conduct recall verification activities for a Class II recall within 5 working days. [fsis_dir_8080_1_r8:20:0]

To keep kitchen equipment in a state of repair and condition that meets the requirements of Parts 4‑1 and 4‑2, the following steps must be followed:  
1. Maintain all equipment in a state of repair and condition that meets the specifications of Parts 4‑1 and 4‑2.  
2. Keep components such as doors, seals, hinges, fasteners, and kick plates intact, tight, and adjusted in accordance with the manufacturer’s specifications.  
3. Keep cutting or piercing parts of can openers sharp to minimize the creation of metal fragments that can contaminate food.  
4. Perform proper maintenance of equipment according to manufacturer specifications to ensure continued operation as designed and to prevent violations that could endanger consumer health.  
[doc_a:4-501.11]

To prevent allergen cross‑contact when using fryer oil in a seafood processing facility, processors should:  
1. Use dedicated fryers for allergen‑containing products (e.g., shrimp) so that the oil is not reused for non‑allergen products, thereby minimizing the risk of protein transfer. [fda_seafood_ch19:2:1]  
2. Implement cleaning and sanitation procedures that effectively remove allergenic proteins from fryer equipment and oil, as part of a broader allergen control program. [fda_seafood_app10:1:1]

IPP must verify that the design of the establishment’s sampling and testing program is adequate when performing the HAV task. If the program is included in a Sanitation SOP, prerequisite program, or HACCP plan, the IPP must review its adequacy during the HAV task. [fsis_dir_10240_4_r4:13:0]

Before monitoring EPIPT, you must:  
1. Conduct a temperature‑distribution study within the heating system to identify any cold spots.  
2. Conduct a heat‑penetration study that accounts for the slowest‑heating product under the worst‑case heating conditions covered by the scientific study.  
3. Identify other critical factors of processing and/or packaging that affect the rate of product heating when scientifically establishing the heat process.  
These steps ensure the EPIPT selected will provide an appropriate reduction (e.g., 6D) of the target pathogen. [fda_pchf_ch04:11:1]

FSIS personnel must first gather relevant information about the product, including contact details for the firms involved in production and distribution, and any data that might affect the scope of the product or mitigate the need for a recall. They should also collect product label information, such as photographs or digital scans, and submit this to RMTAD via email whenever possible. If the District Manager or Regional Director determines the event should be escalated, the assigned personnel must work with the firm to complete and forward a copy of FSIS Form 5020‑3, Preliminary Inquiry Worksheet, to RMTAD for assessment and to create an Agency Report of Adulteration (ARA) in PHIS. The information provided by the firm on Form 5020‑3 must be verified by District or Regional Office personnel before submission. [fsis_dir_8080_1_r8:3:2]

An establishment must review all records associated with the production of the product to confirm that every critical limit has been met and that any required corrective actions have been completed (8a). The review must be performed, dated, and signed by an individual who did not produce the HACCP records, unless the establishment has too few employees to allow this separation (8b). The product is considered “produced and shipped” only after the pre‑shipment review is completed, and the review may be done in stages or at a location other than the producing facility, provided the review of the appropriate documents and compliance with 9 CFR 417.5(c) occurs before the product leaves the control of the producing establishment (8c‑d). [fsis_dir_5000_1_r8:43:0]

To maintain active managerial control over foodborne illness risk factors, a food safety management system must include:  

1. Certified food protection managers who have demonstrated proficiency through accredited testing.  
2. Standard operating procedures (SOPs) for critical operational steps such as cooling.  
3. Recipe cards that specify preparation steps and critical limits (e.g., final cooking temperatures).  
4. Purchase specifications, equipment and facility design and maintenance, and monitoring procedures.  
5. Comprehensive record‑keeping, employee health policies to restrict or exclude ill staff, and ongoing training for managers and employees.  
6. Continuous quality control and assurance activities, including specific goal‑oriented plans such as Risk Control Plans (RCPs) that outline procedures for controlling identified risk factors.  

These elements collectively provide a preventive, continuous system of monitoring and verification that embodies active managerial control.  
[doc_a:563:0, doc_b:12:0]

An establishment should keep its grounds from harboring vermin by ensuring that trash does not accumulate, storing pallets and other equipment properly, and keeping the grounds drained. [fsis_sps_guide:5:1]

A time‑and‑temperature management strategy should keep product temperatures below the minimum growth temperature for each relevant pathogen or, if that is not possible, ensure that the product is not held above that temperature for longer than the pathogen’s lag‑growth phase so that the bacteria do not reach the infectious or toxic dose [fda_seafood_ch12:3:0]. The strategy must also account for cumulative exposure across all processing and storage steps, because repeated or prolonged time‑temperature abuse can allow pathogens to accumulate to unsafe levels even if each individual step is within limits [fda_seafood_ch12:4:3]. In practice, this means establishing critical limits, monitoring procedures, and corrective actions that prevent any significant growth of pathogens such as V. parahaemolyticus, V. vulnificus, S. aureus, B. cereus, C. perfringens, and others before they reach their typical infectious or toxic doses [fda_seafood_ch12:3:0].

To monitor or verify the content of a product label, you must confirm that the label/package you receive from a supplier or generate yourself: (1) satisfies the food allergen label specification you developed for the product; and (2) is the correct label/package for the specific product with its ingredient specification (recipe or formulation). [fda_pchf_ch11:30:1]
Not found in the provided documents.

To determine the appropriate cleaning frequency for equipment and utensils, you should review the sanitary design of the room and equipment, assess the microbiological profile during a production run, examine the history of Listeria spp. in the room and on the line, and consider the degree of product exposure to the line and the environment. These factors help you establish a cleaning schedule that ensures control of L. monocytogenes and minimizes conditions that promote its survival or multiplication. [fda_lm_rte_2017:24:0]

The factors that must be considered include whether conditions during finished product storage and distribution are likely to create a reduced‑oxygen packaging environment that would allow C. botulinum to grow and produce toxin. This assessment also involves evaluating if any preventive measures can eliminate or reduce the hazard to an acceptable level at that processing step. [fda_seafood_ch13:11:1]

A preventive controls qualified individual must conduct or oversee a scientific study that establishes the critical parameters (cooking temperature, time, particle size, and any other critical factors) required to deliver the desired reduction level for products with large particles. The study must demonstrate that if the minimum/maximum values for all critical factors are met, every particle will receive an adequate heat treatment. Once the study is complete, the individual provides the processor with the time and temperature that must be monitored during processing, as well as any other critical parameters. During production the processor must monitor the time and temperature of the heat process (and any other identified critical factors) to ensure all product particles achieve the required internal temperature. If EPIPT is used, it must be based on a validated scientific study that shows the selected EPIPT provides the required reduction under the worst heating conditions. [fda_pchf_ch04:11:0]

The purpose of a firm’s recall effectiveness checks is to verify that all consignees at the recall depth specified by the strategy have received notification about the recall and have taken appropriate action. [fda_rpm_ch07:33:0]

Once in service, a temperature‑indicating device should be checked daily before the beginning of operations. The check must confirm the device’s accuracy (e.g., by comparing its reading to a known accurate reference device or by immersion in a calibrated ice slurry or boiling water as appropriate) and include a visual examination of the sensor and any attached wires for damage or kinks, ensuring the device is operational. [fda_seafood_ch12:15:0]

During a comprehensive investigation of Listeria trends, an establishment should:  
1. Review cleaning and sanitizing procedures, including the types of cleaning agents used, and examine traffic‑control patterns, equipment layout, and employee hygiene compliance. [fsis_lm_rte_2014:123:1]  
2. Identify potential harborage sites by locating niches that may harbor Lm, especially where repeated, non‑consecutive positives occur. [fsis_lm_rte_2014:123:1]  
3. Increase sampling at the positive sites, testing individual pieces of equipment and upstream areas in the production line, collecting 3–5 samples per event until negatives are obtained. [fsis_lm_rte_2014:123:1]  
4. Conduct preventive actions such as intensifying sanitation frequency, repairing or replacing equipment, and reassessing the Sanitation SOP and HACCP program. [fsis_lm_rte_2014:123:0]

Internal product temperatures at delivery should be checked with a temperature‑indicating device (e.g., a thermometer) for each lot that is delivered refrigerated (not frozen) or under chemical cooling media, and for each lot delivered with a transit time of 4 hours or less. For products delivered under ice, visual observation of the adequacy of ice surrounding the product is required, and for products delivered under chemical cooling media a visual check of the cooling media plus a temperature‑indicating device is required. For refrigerated (not frozen) lots, a continuous temperature‑recording device may also be used during transit. [fda_seafood_ch12:12:1] [fda_seafood_ch13:25:0]

Raw meat, poultry and seafood must be cold‑stored separately from work‑in‑progress, processed, cooked and packaged products, with segregation and distinct marking to keep them apart from other materials. [fssai_sched4_compendium:48:0]

Before a temperature‑indicating device is put into service, its accuracy must be verified by checking it against a known accurate reference. This can be done by immersing the sensor in an ice slurry at 32 °F (0 °C) if it will be used at or near refrigeration temperature, or by comparing its reading with that of a NIST‑traceable thermometer under conditions similar to its intended use within the relevant temperature range. [fda_seafood_ch13:27:0]

Carcasses must be transported from the slaughter house to the premises in hygienic conditions, using boxes of adequate size linked with zinc/aluminium/stainless steel or wire gauze meat safes that are washed daily. They should also be transported in insulated refrigerated vans, and must never be carried in vehicles used for commuting people or in an exposed condition. [fssai_sched4_compendium:87:0]

Before the 423(a) letter is sent, the Center must upload into CMS the health‑hazard evaluation (HHE), all expert memos (including those on reasonable probability of adulteration/misbranding and SAHCODHA), supporting evidence such as lab test results, the draft order of nondistribution, and any other required memos or documentation that lay out the legal and factual basis for FDA’s position. [fda_rpm_ch07:77:2, fda_rpm_ch07:79:1]

A written recall plan for food requiring a preventive control must include procedures that describe the steps to be taken and assign responsibility for those steps, and must cover the following actions: (1) directly notify the direct consignees of the food being recalled, including how to return or dispose of the affected food; (2) notify the public about any hazard presented by the food when appropriate to protect public health; (3) conduct effectiveness checks to verify that the recall is carried out; and (4) appropriately dispose of recalled food—e.g., through reprocessing, reworking, diverting to a use that does not present a safety concern, or destroying the food.
